Toxoplasma gondii is one of the major causes of human infection and leads to a wide range of severe diseases such as latent and acute disseminated toxoplasmosis, and the mostly subclinical illness, acute toxoplasmosis. In order to further elucidate the molecular mechanisms contributing to host cell control of toxoplasma pathogenesis, a series of crystal structures of the prezygotal tachyzoite envelope (TPE) as well as the membrane-cytoplasmic junction (M-CJ) domain spanning the cell envelope in the A-type tachyzoite, and the c-type hypervariable glycoprotein transporter (Tht) genes encoding intracellular protein transporter in the pathogenic morphotype of the fungus, were solved by various methods, with different protein mixtures. Comparative genomics and comparative biochemistry with related neurotoxin-producing fungi and yeasts gave important insights on the diversity of TPE synthesis and production, explaining the fact that the prezygotal tachyzoite TPE are multigene family, exhibiting similar patterns of sequence conservation and divergence between species, but with different splice variations and combinations. Comparative proteomic studies showed that there is considerable independent evolution within TPE gene families and this evolution was likely partly associated with increases in enzyme activity with similar effects on the active extracellular subunit. The M-CJ surface is conserved among all tachyzoites, possibly reflecting the conservation of putative intermediate membrane machinery. The c-type hypervariable glycoprotein transporter (Tht) complexes with several but not all known Tpe family transmembrane proteases, which suggests a conserved requirement for the Tht-cofactor from the same family. Among the sequences the crystallization, molecular and biochemical studies has been executed on, structural information could be obtained. The scFv of C-type hypervariable glycoprotein trans-porter (Tht) contains, on the C-termini, the unique conserved triple-HELA and its close related subtetra-HELA and triple-ETLB binding sites, as well as the exception of the K-term which contains an extended cluster of amino acids, distinguishing this structure from those of the other hypervariable Tht chain found so far, which contains the metal-binding region that affects substrate interactions. These studies have high potential to identify novel THT cofactor interactions and complexes.

A novel gold nanotoxoid, ll3CYN, was developed and used in two invasive bacterial infections: an animal bacillus infection, Bacillus pumilis and an animal protozoal infection, Trypanosoma brucei. ll3CYN was initially synthesized as a single-stranded gold (Au) nanoparticle (AuNPs) with sufficient Au content for gold toxicity in a bacterial reaction system.  The activity of ll3CYN as an antibacterial agent was also studied using an in vitro assay in the presence of HeLa cells. As a nontoxic inorganic metallic nanofluids (MFs), ll3CYN enhances the immune response of heat shock mutants induced by exposure to the bacteria. L. pumilis and T. brucei intracellular foci accumulations were blocked by ll3CYN, while no toxic effects were seen in HeLa cells.  Given that ll3CYN has strong cytotoxicity against other bacterial strains, we then tested this nanomide as a man-made molecular adjuvant.  In a model prion disease model, LLN-C Pr529L demonstrates effective adjuvant activity against a visible increase in disease severity in specific experimental organisms.  These agents complement natural bio-based immune responses and thus hold therapeutic potential in various disease models.

HighlightsFirst reported Ll3CYN used in experimental animal infections to treat an array of bacterial diseases

Legionellosis is a ubiquitous infection that causes severe disease in many animals worldwide and can cause subclinical infection in humans. However, little is known about the impact of Legionellae causing infection on reproduction or infection dynamics in white-tailed deer. Here, we used public genomic datasets from two northern Wisconsin deer hosts to study doxycycline treatment in the deer's reproductive and blood systems. We observed declines in luteal and follicular cell percentage in the Deer Lop and Deer Mohawk male hosts relative to the Wild European white-tailed deer (EW). However, these effects were negligible when comparing male Deer Potlach and Deer Wapiti hosts. In both species, doxycycline treatment showed no significant effects on fertility or development during natural cycles. Sexual maturity was improved, with the natural deer cohort exceeding and exceeding the colony average for the steroidogenic pathway and the F9 ovary androgen receptor. However, it was less mature and hormone concentrations were more unpredictable. These results suggest that dacron is a viable option for limiting new infections in deer. Moreover, we discuss the findings of recent metagenomic studies of white-tailed deer, in which the first white-tailed deer genomic dataset was deposited in 2023. In these studies, gene counts associated with photosynthesis in these deer hosts were high compared to other deer species, including Beta-carotene pathway genes, carotenoid biosynthesis pathways, and carotenoids.

Chlamydia trachomatis infections are one of the most prevalent infectious causes of neonatal blindness worldwide. In addition to antibiotic therapies, the prompt availability of an effective prevention vaccine could greatly improve the global health situation. With funding from the Foundation Fighting Blindness Thailand 2020 International Challenge Grant, a worldwide team led by Cagnotto established a collaborative scientific consortium, including collaborators from Thailand and the Center for Urogenital Infections, Antibiotic Resistance and Virus Prevention at Cochin University. Our primary goal is to generate the clinical evidence for a successful prophylactic vaccine to reduce cervical-associated C. trachomatis infections, especially in Thailand, where the incidence of HIV-associated cervical-associated C. trachomatis infections (C-AC-CTIs) is high. Initial data provide preclinical support for the design of a prophylactic cervical vaccine in partnership with South Korea and Singapore. This project seeks to apply such vaccine technology to a treatment of the strongest pressingly needed cervical-associated C. trachomatis infections in Thai neonates and to the treatment of newborns from Cambodia and Myanmar, which have similarly high incidence rates, via virus-like particle (VLP) vaccines, of HIV-associated CTIs. While a long-term study is required to determine the clinical and socio-economic impact of VLP cervical vaccines in Thailand, to inform vaccine development for the regions of high C. trachomatis infection incidence, we design and achieve the first step towards VLP cervical vaccines for Thailand and Myanmar based on Thailand's SARS-CoV-2 vaccination efforts. Keywords Clostridia​infection, congenitalCervicalCommunication (CAC), Pre-clinical study, Viral-like Particles (VLP), Prevention, Pregnancy

Brodectinomycosis, a rare, multi-drug resistant infection caused by Borrelia burgdorferi-the etiological agent of Lyme borreliosis, is often characterized as a wound-healing infection. However, the host response to borreliosis is not solely dependent on the level of wound healing. In this study we define a host immune response in response to BOR2-infected mice. We show that an over-expression of the receptor for Borrelia burgdorferi receptor for Toll like (ROTLL), the innate immune receptor upregulated by BOR2 infection, attenuates borreliosis. A strain of mice expressing a null genotype for the innate immune receptor TAG2 (trafficking 2) as a reporter also demonstrated a low RH(OC)-borrelia and a decreased ROS signal compared to their wildtype controls. An augmented COAT1-tag5 + RO1-tag4 allele combination harboring C:AGDNA codons code for both the rot of the PIN-FORMED protein, a target protein of both RIG-I and TOLL like receptors, and the binding site for the tag18 transcript of the granulocyte macrophage colony stimulating factor (GM-CSF) subunit. RIG-I and toLL2 cells were also upregulated at increased levels. To understand how the host innate immune responses are established, and to determine if mouse models are suitable for drug-development, we isolated small biofilm-like residues in E. coli BglK mutant strains expressing antibodies to the immune receptors recognized by B. burgdorferi receptor for Toll-like receptors (ROTLLL and TAG2), and observed lower resistance against BOR2 in RLT2-positive strains. The results indicate that microorganisms in organ-waste, considered the major reservoir for BOR2 transmission, or the infectious agents of Lyme borreliosis, undergo a selective divergence due to the pathogen itself.

Leptospira infection during the early postnatal life plays a major role in the acquisition of lifelong immunity. Here, we tested for a comprehensive cross-immunity in mice on an initial infection with the invasive pathogen Leptospira serogroup B. 25, a causative pathogen of leptospirosis in Brazil, and the subsequent transmission of the infection from the mother. At 16 days of age, the offspring had an antibody response in the urinary tract. The titres of IgG in the blood were significantly higher in the vaccinated group as compared to the non-vaccinated group. The titres remained higher in animals who received two or three injections of leptospira serogroup B, with severe disease. Following the third leptospirosis vaccination, mice developed an effective anti-Ser B antibody response. A five-factor haplotype explained the best and the strongest cross-immunity.

Rickettsiae are intracellular bacterial agents of animal health. A number of pathogenic species have evolved intracellular vectors that exert an obligate predatory role in the host intestine, which enables them to reduce grazing in the mucosa. Stomula aerophilus (formerly Zoothamnion hoary) and Tetranychus (formerly Mulinus curtisii) are two major contributors to rickettsial pathology. In contrast, V. Caesalpiniae (Rickettsia alangerorum) -- a nematode obligate parasite -- does not colonize either host intestine but exerts an obligate predatory role in the host metacercariae rather than invading tissue. Both amoeboid lice and Megathura affinis (formerly Notomunoides vernu) are strictly parasitic, but their predatory mode is less understood. With these studies we propose that amoeboid lice and Megathura affinis serve as the definitive reservoirs of vitamin B12 in the megaera alga Spirogyra, and that parasite-free larval alga feeds on symbiotic V. caesalpiniae via them.

Factoring these findings, we propose that parasites create an obligate predatory, parasitic relationship with the megaera alga Spirogyra, able to circumvent the need to move to other host tissues as rickettsiae do. Such a shift in parasite ecology is theologically parallel to how pre-Christian-era Christian theologians interpreted the Gospel.

BackgroundLyme borreliosis (LBL) is one of the most common tick-borne zoonotic diseases worldwide. The pathogenesis of LBL and the toxic effects caused by LBL do not appear to be well understood and there are no approved therapies for LBL. Here we investigate the mechanism of action of LBL in this parasitic disease.

MethodsWe screened a compound library with verified mycoparasite suppression activity, using the strain of Borrelia burgdorferi, which causes Lyme borreliosis, to identify LBL specific targets. Based on known biological mechanisms of action, an “activator” was found to counteract the toxic effects of LBL by increasing IL-12 expression and growth inhibition in noculture and lyme disease model mice. We identified many antibodies specific for activated IL-12 that directly bind to IL-12 in lyme disease model mice and activated neutrophils. These antibodies appear to play important roles in the antitumor immune response mediated by IL-12.

ResultsWe identified and experimentally verified an anticancer drug based on a specific antibody, a molecularly linked molecule, secreted from activated neutrophils. This new molecular anticancer drug, LYN, inhibited LBL growth effectively in noculture and lyme disease model mice and has demonstrated anticancer activity in a lyme disease model mouse. The anticancer drug LYN also had specific antifungal, antiviral and immunosuppressant activities that counteracted the pathogenesis of lyme borreliosis. The mechanism of action and structure of LYN were first evaluated in lyme disease model mice. Results from molecular imaging experiments revealed that the structure of LYN had hydrophobic, positive dielectric anisotropy in the crystalline state, and a hydrophobic/positive dielectric anisotropy in its microdomain oligomers. In contrast to molecular weight dependent mode of action, LYN affected the well-established signal transduction pathways involved in the growth of lyme borreliosis in tissues using lyme disease model mice. Inhibitors of the IL-12/IL-18 signaling pathway, such as irinotecan or damine were not sufficient in inhibiting LBL growth in lyme disease model mice. This study provides new insights into the molecular mechanism of action of lyme borreliosis, and the chemical properties of the drug LYN, providing a novel molecular target for the development of targeted therapeutic and anti-leprosy drug, LYN.

Pellegriniella multicystiaca represents a rare and morphologically complex leishmanial species, restricted to humans but present in some rodents, birds, and bats. It is considered to be a possible source of several Leishmania species. We report the presence of a PCR sub-error in the Leishmania interrogans index (LdTI), an interspecies Leishmania isololating strategy widely used to identify isolates of Leishmania sp. from large fragments of fecal samples from patients colonized by Leishmania-infected blood. To detect PCR errors, we sequenced 10 different leishmania sequences sampled over a long period of time and simultaneously for all LdTI criteria, identifying an error rate of 0.12%. By careful analysis, we conclude that most leishmaniases with PCR errors may be attributed to the inability to purify isolated leishmania from the search specimens, therefore suggesting that isolation of LdTI and PCR amplification are not always adequate. Despite PCR errors in other leishmania species, such as DrPibophila and Dr.divaricans, our study on LdTI is the first observation of this problem in a true PCR strategy from new strains previously described as isolated from humans and poorly characterized.

Gastrointestinal helminths interact with multiple immune cells, highlighting the complex interplay between innate immunity and host resilience. Meta-analysis revealed that macrophages were primarily affected by helminth infection. Anti-helminthic therapies mainly target macrophages for full efficacy. Here, we characterize the underlying mechanisms of helminth immunity in vivo that affect infection immunity and show that helminth immunity in mice is marked by an acute infection model. Experiments with helminths of various species confirmed that helminth infections strongly suppress the innate immune response in infected mice, providing a novel insight into the role of helminth disease resistance. When helminths infected the immature immune system, an enhanced innate immune response was observed, leading to an anti-inflammatory phenotype. This leads to a stronger antiviral response mediated by infected cells which can promote development of innate immunity. However, in the non-immune population, helminths can generate an over-activated innate immune response resulting in harmful alterations. These experiments demonstrate the importance of the innate immune response in the context of helminth infection.
sample_p_texts: Balamuthia mandrillaris is a free-living amoeba that can infect the central nervous system to cause granulomatous amebic encephalitis (GAE), a highly fatal disease with mortality rates up to 90%. GAE is typically treated with a six-drug regimen with limited efficacy and significant toxicity. Our lab previously identified nitroxoline, a quinolone antibiotic, as a promising therapeutic complement to the existing regimen, and in 2021 nitroxoline was first successfully used to treat a human patient. In this study, we elucidate nitroxolines mechanism of action using a combination of genomics, transcriptomics, chemical complementation, growth assays, and electron microscopy. In service of this goal, an annotated draft genome of B. mandrillaris strain CDC:V039 was generated using long read sequencing, yielding 88 telomere-to-telomere contigs and over 25,000 protein coding genes. Leveraging this resource, comparative transcriptomics were used to characterize encystment responses to three different cellular stressors: nitroxoline, galactose, and hypoxia. Our findings reveal that nitroxoline-induced cysts undergo transcriptional collapse and genomic and structural destabilization via copper and iron chelation. These data provide insight into nitroxolines multifaceted impact on B. mandrillaris growth and cellular processes and advance our understanding of the transcriptional landscape associated with stress induced encystment. Our findings support the continued clinical study of nitroxoline.

Ivermectin (IVM), an antiparasitic drug, was repurposed to treat COVID-19 based on its in vitro antiviral effects. However, it was abandoned after multiple clinical trials reported a lack of efficacy. Immunomodulatory effects have been proposed but remain unclear, yet they may be relevant given IVM use for other infections. We assessed the IVM immunomodulatory effect in 24 participants from a clinical trial evaluating its potential to reduce COVID-19 transmission in mild cases within 48 hours of symptoms onset. The IVM-treated patients showed non-significant lower viral loads, and a significantly shorter duration of hyposmia/anosmia. We measured IgG, IgA, and IgM against five SARS-CoV-2 antigens, and 30 cytokines by Luminex, alongside whole blood RNA sequencing, pan-leukocyte immunophenotyping, and SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell analysis by flow cytometry from day 1 to day 28 post-treatment. All antibody responses increased from day 4, while 13 cytokines significantly decreased over time (adjusted p<0.05). IVM-treated patients had only significantly higher anti-nucleocapsid IgG levels at day 4 (adjusted p=0.041) and 7 (adjusted p=0.045) compared to placebo. SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cells increased over time, with significantly higher effector memory CD4+ T cells at day 7 compared to day 1 (p=0.027) and the only difference between groups was lower frequencies of spike-specific naive CD4+ T cells at day 7 in IVM-treated participants (0.006% vs 0.036% p=0.02). Transcriptomic data showed downregulation of innate and antiviral blood transcriptional modules (BTMs) over time, with an increase in adaptive immune related BTMs. While no differential gene expression was detected, the IVM-treated had upregulated innate and downregulated T cell and cell cycle BTMs compared to placebo. Overall, our comprehensive longitudinal analysis of early immune responses in mild COVID-19 revealed no robust immunological effects of IVM, consistent with clinical trials results and suggesting a lack of efficacy of IVM in COVID-19 treatment.

AUTHOR SUMMARYIvermectin (IVM), an antiparasitic drug, was tested in clinical trials as a potential treatment for COVID-19 due to its in vitro antiviral properties and hypothetical immunomodulatory effects. In this study, we explored the immunomodulatory effects of IVM in a clinical trial involving 24 mild COVID-19 patients who received IVM within 48 hours of symptoms onset. The IVM group showed a trend towards lower viral loads post-treatment, and a significantly shorter duration of hyposmia/anosmia. We comprehensively analyzed immune responses by measuring antibody levels, cytokine profiles, immune cell subsets and whole blood gene expression over 28 days. The IVM group only had increased levels of IgG against the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid compared to the control group. IVM did not affect the kinetics of SARS-CoV-2 T cells, despite a slight decrease in naive CD4+ T cells. Additionally, gene expression analysis showed a decrease in innate and antiviral responses and an increase of adaptive responses over time that were slightly stronger in the placebo compared to the IVM group. In conclusion, despite some differences in IVM treated participants, our detailed analyses do not support significant immunomodulatory effects that could benefit disease progression.

Babesiosis is a disease brought on by intraerythrocytic parasites of the genus Babesia. Current chemotherapies are accompanied by side effects and parasite relapse. Therefore, it is crucial to develop highly effective drugs against Babesia. Cipargamin (CIP) has shown inhibition against apicomplexan parasites, mainly Plasmodium and Toxoplasma. This study evaluated the growth-inhibiting properties of CIP against Babesia spp. and investigated the mechanism of CIP on B. gibsoni. The half inhibitory concentration (IC50) values of CIP against the in vitro growth of B. bovis and B. gibsoni were 20.2 {+/-} 1.4 nM and 69.4 {+/-} 2.2 nM, respectively. CIP significantly inhibited the growth of B. microti and B. rodhaini in vivo. Resistance was conferred by L921V and L921I mutations in BgATP4, which reduced the sensitivity to CIP by 6.1- and 12.8-fold. The inhibitory potency of CIP against BgATP4-associated ATPase activity was moderately reduced in mutant strains, with a 1.3-fold and 2.4-fold decrease in BgATP4L921V and BgATP4L921I, respectively, compared to that of BgATP4WT. An in silico investigation revealed reductions in affinity for CIP binding to BgATP4L921V and BgATP4L921I compared to BgATP4WT. Resistant strains showed no significant cross-resistance to atovaquone (ATO) or tafenoquine succinate (TQ), with less than a onefold change in IC50 values. Combining CIP with TQ effectively eliminated B. microti infection in SCID mice with no relapse, and parasite DNA was not detected by qPCR within 90 days post-infection. Our findings reveal the efficacy of CIP as an anti-babesial agent, its limitations as a monotherapy due to resistance development, and the potential of combination therapy with TQ to overcome said resistance and achieve complete parasite clearance.

Leptospirosis is a neglected zoonotic disease caused by pathogenic Leptospira spp., affecting an estimated of one million people annually and resulting in approximately 60,000 fatalities. The disease can lead to hepatic, renal, and pulmonary dysfunctions and may contribute to the development of chronic kidney disease.

The Complement System plays a crucial role in eliminating bacteria by generating opsonins, anaphylotoxins, that degranulate mastocytes and basophils, and attract immune cells to the infection site, among other important functions.

This study aimed to investigate the role of C3, the central protein of the Complement System, in vivo during chronic infection of L interrogans serovar Copenhageni strain FIOCRUZ L1-130 (LIC). C57BL/6 wild-type (WT) and C3 knockout (C3KO) mice were infected with 108 LIC and monitored at 15, 30, 60, 90 and 180 days post-infection (d.p.i.).

LIC-infected C3KO mice exhibited a significantly higher leptospiral load in the kidneys compared to WT counterparts. Both groups showed local inflammation at 15 and 30 d.p.i., but only C3KO LIC-infected mice had a higher number of Leptospira DNA copies at 30 d.p.i. At the same time point, C3KO LIC-infected mice developed a larger fibrotic area than WT mice. Interestingly, independent of C3, mice pre-treated with a nephrotoxic drug increased the renal inflammatory response; however, this pretreatment did not affect the local leptospiral load in infected mice. Additionally, levels of specific IgG2b and IgG3 antibodies were significantly higher in LIC-infected C3KO mice compared to WT mice.

Proteomic analysis showed lower levels of C5/C5a in WT and C3KO LIC-infected mice, as well as in C3KO control mice. M-CSF and SDF-1 cytokine levels were reduced in both LIC-infected groups. Furthermore, naive T lymphocytes count (both CD4+ and CD8+) were higher in LIC-infected C3KO mice, whereas effector CD8+ T lymphocyte numbers declined during LIC infection - a phenomenon more pronounced in C3KO mice.

Overall, this study demonstrates that during LIC infection, the absence of C3 does not affect mouse survival but leads to increased renal leptospiral load and fibrosis. Additionally, it highlights the crucial role of C3 in supporting the maturation and differentiation of T lymphocytes into pre-effector cells, underscoring its importance as a key link between the innate and adaptive immune responses in leptospirosis.

Author SummaryLeptospirosis is an infectious disease with approximately one million new cases annually and is responsible for about 5% of deaths, particularly in underdeveloped countries. Our objective is to understand the immune response in leptospirosis, specifically the role of the Complement C3 protein. In this study, we observed that C3 deficiency is associated with a higher renal leptospiral load and an increased incidence of renal fibrosis after one month of chronic infection. Notably, C3 also influences the differentiation of helper and cytotoxic T lymphocytes into effector cells, potentially contributing to the increased severity of chronic leptospirosis observed in C3-deficient animals.

BackgroundIn Leishmania-endemic areas, humans are chronically exposed to the bites of vector sand flies, whose immunogenic salivary proteins modulate host immunity. The immune consequences of this chronic antigenic exposure remain poorly understood.

ObjectiveTo characterize bite-induced rash and cytokine responses to sand fly salivary proteins in humans chronically exposed to Lutzomyia longipalpis, the main vector of visceral leishmaniasis in the Americas.

MethodsWe conducted a controlled human vector challenge study, exposing 15 healthy volunteers to Lutzomyia longipalpis bites multiple times over a year. We assessed bite site skin reactions and stimulated peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) with salivary gland extract or two immunogenic Lutzomyia longipalpis salivary proteins, LJM19 and LJL143, to measure cytokine responses and macrophage killing of Leishmania.

ResultsBite sites developed pruritic, erythematous papules consistent with a delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) response. PBMCs stimulated with LJM19 or LJL143 elicited TH1-polarized cytokine responses and high expression of the TH2 cytokine IL-13. LJM19 increased levels of IL-6 and IL-7, while both proteins stimulated IL-1{beta} and IFN- production. LJM19- and LJL143-mediated parasite killing by macrophages correlated with TH1 polarization. LJM19 also enhanced Leishmania killing in cells from individuals unexposed to Lutzomyia longipalpis. Two participants exhibited prominent bite site infiltration with CD4-CD8-T cells.

ConclusionsChronic exposure to sand fly bites elicits a DTH response and induces innate and adaptive cytokine responses to salivary proteins that correlate with enhanced Leishmania killing. Controlled human vector challenge studies are valuable for investigating the immunologic mechanisms driven by long-term exposure to vector salivary antigens.

Tick-borne diseases are a growing public health concern in the United States, with cases rising steadily each year. Lyme borreliosis, or Lyme disease, remains the most prevalent, affecting approximately 476,000 individuals annually. Human-driven changes in climate and ecosystems have expanded the habitat of pathogen-carrying ticks, facilitating the spread of these infections. Additionally, increased instances of tick-borne diseases transmission through human tissues have been reported. Despite ongoing efforts to manage these infections, their incidence continues to rise. To develop effective control measures against these diseases and prevent the transmission of tick-borne infections through human and animal tissues, it is very important to develop detection assays and understand the transmission mechanisms of tick-borne infections. In this study, we provide detailed descriptions and visual references for larval and nymphal tick feeding on mice, focusing on the transmission and acquisition of Borrelia burgdorferi (sensu stricto). These methodologies can be applied to study other tick-borne diseases, tick vectorial capacity, and tick biology, aiding in the development of detection strategies to combat these infections.

Soil-transmitted helminths, like Ascaris, are significant contributors to disease burden in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Infections are associated with growth faltering and mortality in children and are often transmitted through contact with eggs in fecally contaminated soil. Interventions, like replacing household soil floors with cement-based alternatives, may reduce exposure to Ascaris eggs, but there are currently no estimates on the removal or survival of Ascaris eggs on cement-based surfaces. This study addresses that knowledge gap by evaluating the removal of Ascaris eggs from mopping and the survival of Ascaris eggs on two cement-based mixes: an Ordinary Portland Cement (OPC) mortar and an OPC mortar with fly ash, which provides a more sustainable alternative to the OPC mortar mix. We assessed egg survival at two temperatures representing the dry (15{degrees}C) and wet (34{degrees}C) seasons in Bangladesh using two different egg enumeration methods. After mopping, over 92% of viable eggs were removed from surfaces, with no significant differences between cement-based mixes (p = 0.51). The first-order decay rate constants (k) of Ascaris eggs were similar between mix designs (p = 0.62) but varied significantly between temperatures (p = 4.2 x 10-25) and egg enumeration methods (p = 2.4 x 10-8). The k values were of greater magnitude at 34{degrees}C compared to at 15{degrees}C. At 15{degrees}C, k values were not significantly different from zero, indicating no inactivation. The k values we obtained were comparable to those reported in previous studies for different matrices, indicating comparable inactivation of Ascaris eggs on cement-based surfaces compared to liquid and semi-solid matrices. These results provide some of the first estimates of removal efficiencies and inactivation times in realistic environmental conditions for Ascaris on surfaces while supporting the use of OPC mortar mix designs with fly ash in interventions to reduce Ascaris transmission in rural LMIC households.

Author SummarySoil-transmitted helminths, like Ascaris, are parasites that are major contributors to disease in children and women of childbearing age in low- and middle-income countries. Interventions, like replacing soil floors in households with cement-based flooring, may reduce exposure to Ascaris eggs which cause infections, but there is little information on how or why these interventions may be effective. This study investigates the effectiveness of simple cleaning methods, like mopping, in removing Ascaris eggs from cement-based surfaces and explores how long these eggs can survive on these surfaces under different environmental conditions. We tested two types of cement-based surfaces, a traditional cement-based mortar mix, and a more sustainable cement-based mortar mix, and found that mopping removed over 92% of Ascaris eggs, with no differences between cement mixes. Experiments simulating wet and dry seasonal conditions showed that Ascaris eggs survive longer in cooler environments, again with no differences between cement mixes. These findings provide important insights into the role of cement-based flooring in interrupting disease transmission and suggest sustainable cement-based mortar mixes are a feasible alternative to traditional cement-based mortar mixes.

Cancer remains the leading cause of death worldwide. Scientists have applied different integrative data sources (e.g., genomics, immune gene expression, imaging, immune cells) to identify biomarkers and design personalized prevention and treatment strategies. However, how to optimally integrate both human and animal data remains a challenge. To overcome this problem, we introduce a pathway inference model which combines omics data, such as genomic and immune signatures, and behavioral response data such as risk profiles and anthropometric measurements. We also construct a comprehensive molecular clustering network, for which we introduce new labels and calculated structural properties. This combined dataset forms the basis of our model, termed Integrative Molecular Networks and Pathways Inference (IMNI). We establish that genomic profiles jointly extract substantial information with behavioral factors. Moreover, we extend our model to complex time-series data through the integration of multiple omics studies, and the inclusion of the acquisition of human samples into the model. We show that the model integrates high precision data and offers much stronger classification performance compared with existing literature. Our work highlights the value of integrated omics models and provides scientists with a framework and source of data to identify effective biomarkers and drug treatment strategies for cancer patients.

Highlights

Importantly, our model also integrates highly complex high-precision data to predict disease prognosis.

Our model was extensively tested and validated with simulated data, including organoid data, 3D brain models, proteomic assays, and Raman spectroscopy.

Discovery of biomarkers remains a significant challenge in functional genomics studies aimed at uncovering biological pathways and cellular functions. While SNP genotyping methodologies have progressed, they often fail to identify alterations not encoded in 3'-5' splice sites, particularly for key proteins like KAT, HAC, and NKX3.2. Consequently, researchers often employ quantitative multiplexed DNA microarrays, often limiting insights into specific disease phenotypes, primarily due to a lack of training samples. Here, we introduce KEClone, a system that extracts, annotates, and analyzes potential multi-analyte splicing-derived signatures for identifying splice-site mutations. This approach employs quantitative methylation profiling of two-way connected KBrIP-plex gene fusions to distinguish splicing mutations and to extract discrete, biostatically detected splice-site mutations to be analyzed by diverse biological assays. The approach presented here enables the biostatistically and functionally relevant identification of splice-site mutations as a foundational method for neurodegenerative and neurological diseases discovery.

The ubiquitous human protein-encoding transcriptome of the human germline is highly variable and should be decoupled from processes such as X-chromosome inactivation (XCI), which is currently the most studied disruption in human gene expression. Here, we analyze the human total RNA transcriptome using transcriptome-wide approaches in an existing cohort of 52,729 patients and 1,805 individuals, where deletion and amplifications were included to create a special subset of homozygous individuals. We analyzed the features of each of these individuals using a highly stable feature classifier. Subsequently, we created and validated a consortium-wide classifier that we used to compute predictions about disease-related genes across all five predicted gene trajectories. We then used the features from the prognostic classifier to predict each disease-related gene and examined the association between gene features and disease-related genes. The results indicated that features were distinctly associated with mutations in genes related to lymphoproliferative disease, intraocular tumors, diabetes, cytokeratin-expressing tumors, skin cancer, prostate cancer, common diseases, atherosclerosis, and multiple other diseases, which also included physical and mental health disorders. The prognostic classifier predicted patients with low features for risk, whereas features of mixed-allelic patients were related to higher risk. Furthermore, we identified genetic disease gene features from associations between gene features and putative, prognostic datasets within the Consortium of Complement Component Polymorphisms (CCPs), and several cohort-specific features. These predictions are important for improving the Precision Health Network (PHN) platform, a global consortium of eNCODE projects that aims to define the large and large-scale human transcriptome and its features, comprising over 300 million full-length human genes that has sequenced about half of the population.

The function of non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) is controversial as most are frequently silenced or mutated, making their overall functions unclear. However, RNA-seq in the human brain revealed that the expression level of ncRNAs differs between healthy and cancer patients. Here, a single gene microarray approach is demonstrated to be accurate for gene expression detection in the human brain, based on the discovery of lncRNA genes associated with cancer, such as high (23.56-fold), high-sensitive (33.04-fold) and very high (52.07-fold) amplification of (BRCA1), (BRCA2) and (PALB2) genes, as a surrogate for potential genomic instability. Furthermore, co-occurrence of genes involved in gene transcription, RNA processing and RNA processing-related functions in the human brain was predicted using different gene clustering algorithms. Most human disease is at the molecular level associated with specific genes that are expressed in a specified tissue. Many such genes are easily sequenced, but identifying their tissuespecific expression changes from organ to tissue requires the use of human organoid technology. Here, we describe the process of using artificially produced human skeletal muscle (HMS) biopsies to assess tissue-specific expression of well-established candidate DNA-binding transcriptional factors. Here we used RNA sequencing data from two different human skeletal muscle biopsies of varying anatomical locations and quantified gene expression changes using two techniques. We used linear discriminant analysis to evaluate candidate expression changes by type of skeletal muscle. The efficacy of this method showed that we can identify changes as many as six times greater than we could obtain with our state-of-the-art RNA-Seq data by evaluating only the main COGs in the 1,000,000-gene complete gene set and the stage-specific promoter networks. The current approach may provide valuable additional sources of molecular information for human skeletal muscle and future applications.

Additionally, several indicators such as BAT-related transcript, telomere, ACTA2, REBGPD, and galactosyltransferase 1C were found to have a functional impact on mortality with this genome feature model. Additionally, our data suggest the use of TELERA as a potential predictor for NAD+ levels in healthy young and elderly adults from the same age group. Thus, our methodology was shown to be a complementary approach to identify trade-off traits.

Hereditary hypertrophic erythropoiesis (HHE) is an inherited, chronic, metabolic disorder characterized by unregulated red blood cell production and intravascular hemolysis, often triggered by infection or inflammation. A growing body of work has discovered new molecular drivers for this condition, including cholesterol, folate, magnesium, testosterone, and others that coordinate erythroid proliferation and maturation, drive oncogenesis, and alter the activity of pre-existing proteins involved in heme biogenesis. Understanding the specific genes and pathways that define HHE will enable the development of early, non-invasive tests, guide drug therapy, and develop new molecular-level diagnostic approaches. Through characterization of genes and pathways involved in erythroid differentiation, we hypothesize that the following drivers are likely associated with HHE: (1) the histidine transporter HCTR1B, a novel nucleotide transporter for transferring ammonium ions into hemoglobin in adult red blood cells; (2) the androgen receptor and steroid hormone receptors; (3) genes important for controlling erythropoiesis including eif4f6b; (4) genes involved in heme biosynthesis including BDHA, ABP, BMP, and ARHGEF1; and (5) X chromosome 1 (Xp) genes, which accumulate due to X-chromosome deletions. While there are currently no approved genetic tests for HHE, the combination of mRNA sequencing and single-cell RNA sequencing could yield a bioinformatic strategy to identify potential genotypes and medications that can be tested in future diagnostic, clinical, and pre-clinical drug studies. Additionally, single-cell transcriptomics and array comparative genomics could be effective tools to understand cellular interactions and their evolutionary changes in different HHE strains.

We determined the gene-centric causative mutations in mutations in discrete genes and identified new genetic associations for each gene. We tested whether homozygous mutations are shared among samples in a population. Through a cohort of patients identified via HEBRA, we introduced an RNA-seq screening combined with deep transcriptomics to study pathways relating to HHE. In this cohort, we identified new genetic associations for each gene with expression across the genome and investigated how this associated genetic mutations affect cell-cycle progression, erythropoiesis, hemoglobin production, and distribution. Here we provided single-cell data for selected genes that were associated with HHE traits and described pathways in all HHE strains, including novel genes identified in the blood transcriptome. Genomic features in humans derived from human genomes and variants associated with prostate cancer have been reported in large-scale genome-wide association studies. However, the risk of prostate cancer is highly heterogeneous among individuals; studies have been hampered by small sample sizes and poor genetic admixture data. With the updated whole-genome sequencing (WGS) technology, human sequence variation can be resolved at a highly individual resolution and with high admixture, which can help solve these issues. We conducted the largest population-scale genomic analysis to date, including samples from more than 32,000 individuals, for prostate cancer and its comorbidity with benign prostate hyperplasia (BPH) and Androgen Deprivation Therapy (ADT). Combining the incidental genetic associations of this cohort with the published human genome and variants association studies (GWAS) from the European Research Consortium on Prostate Cancer (ERC-P2), we identified 26 genomic loci for prostate cancer independently associated with Androgen Deprivation Therapy. We also identified 29 loci associated with prostate cancer and BPH independently associated with the presence of testosterone, with several genes including PEX2, MSH2, MCF83F, and IM1. Taking into account 38 additive model sets, we considered the missing secondary effect and separately found a loss of several associations and an enrichment of others in the presence of the hormone test. These results further confirmed the identification of genetic associations for prostate cancer and BPH for each and every individual, showing the suitability of human whole-genome sequencing as a platform to study complex diseases.

Genomic knowledge and sequence variant data from paralogous genes have been utilized to describe the dysregulated biology of cancers in whole-genome scans. The methods used for high-throughput orthology (HTO) variant prediction fall short when generating functional variants or differential effects from gene mis-regulation in cancer, necessitating the need for more advanced analysis. Hierarchical multigenomic tumor profiling incorporates genetic, clinical and metabolomic features to improve the detection and specificity of cancer-related conditions. Metabolomics can be used to develop diagnostic panels for interventional disease management and proteomics is a valuable tool for disease biomarker identification and multi-omics data manipulation. Integrating metabolomics and proteomics data into genomic analysis provides a comprehensive view of protein function and the mechanisms of disease. This study aims to demonstrate a new approach to this integrative analysis of gene expression, proteomics and metabolomics data by developing a high-throughput variant detection tool.

Methods

• This interdisciplinary analysis was accomplished using two pipeline approaches: MD-profiler to estimate protein function and AMOEBA to detect regulatory states.
• This approach represents a novel way to integrate functional genomics and proteomic data to predict protein dysregulation in cancers and predict the tumor microenvironment for oncology-drug development.

In this study, we developed a high-throughput CDKN2A functional assay and characterized all possible CDKN2A missense variants. We found that 17.7% of all missense variants were functionally deleterious. We also used our functional classifications to assess the performance of in silico models that predict the effect of variants, including recently reported models based on machine learning. Notably, we found that all in silico models performed similarly when compared to our functional classifications with accuracies of 39.5-85.4%. Furthermore, while we found that functionally deleterious variants were enriched within ankyrin repeats, we did not identify any residues where all missense variants were functionally deleterious. Our functional classifications are a resource to aid the interpretation of CDKN2A variants and have important implications for the application of variant interpretation guidelines, particularly the use of in silico models for clinical variant interpretation.

Understanding the genetic regulation of RNA abundance is essential to defining disease mechanisms. However, conventional expression quantitative loci (eQTL) studies quantify RNA molecules across the transcript lifecycle. While most eQTL likely affect transcription by altering promoter or enhancer function within the nucleus, it is also possible that they modulate any processes after transcription, including chemical modifications and RNA stability in the cytosol. To elucidate distinct eQTL mechanisms of early versus late RNA, we compared eQTL from mature cellular RNA and nascent nuclear RNA in the brain and the kidney. Across tissues, we identified different causal variants for cellular and nuclear eQTL for the same eGene. Cellular eQTL were enriched in transcribed regions (P=3.3x10-126), suggesting the importance of post-transcriptional regulation. Conversely, nuclear eQTL were enriched in distal regulatory elements (P=7.0x10-32), highlighting the role of DNA transcriptional regulation. For example, we identified stop-gain eQTL variants likely acting through nonsense-mediated decay in cellular eQTL that had no effect in nuclear eQTL. Cellular eQTL were enriched for loci with multiple causal variants in linkage disequilibrium within the transcribed regions, where they may in concert affect RNA stability. We also identified examples of nuclear eQTL variants within enhancers that had no effect in cellular eQTL. We show that such eQTL (e.g., TUBGCP4) sometimes uniquely colocalize with disease alleles (schizophrenia). This study reveals key differences in the genetic mechanisms of cellular and nuclear eQTL.

Variants of uncertain significance (VUS) are genetic variations with unclear clinical implications, often complicating clinical management in genetic testing. The analysis of co-segregation of the variant with the disease in families has been shown to be a powerful tool for the classification of these variants. We present CAL-Leiden (Co-segregation Analysis via Likelihood ratio analysis-Leiden), a comprehensive co-segregation model facilitating the classification of variants in BRCA1, BRCA2 and PALB2 genes, which can be used as an important component of the ACMG/AMP classification guideline. CAL-Leiden includes an expanded range of cancer types, including pancreatic cancer, in addition to breast and ovarian cancer. It also considers contralateral breast cancer. The model integrates population incidence rates from the Netherlands and the United Kingdom, along with penetrance data from the latest literature. A web-based platform has been developed, making the model accessible and practical for use in diagnostic labs: https://bioexp.net/cosegregation/. We demonstrate the functionality of the tool with multiple pedigrees and compare its performance with alternative approaches. These features in CAL-Leiden collectively contribute to a more comprehensive and accurate assessment of variant pathogenicity, helping lab specialists in classification of the variants of uncertain significance.

Understanding how genetic variation affects tissue structure and function is crucial for deciphering disease mechanisms, yet comprehensive methods for genetic analysis of tissue histology are lacking. We address this gap with HistoGWAS, a framework integrating AI tools for representation learning and image generation with fast variance component models to enable scalable and interpretable genome-wide association studies of histological traits. HistoGWAS employs histology foundation models for automated trait characterization and generative models to visually interpret the genetic influences on these traits. Applied to eleven tissue types from the GTEx cohort, HistoGWAS identifies four genome-wide significant loci, which we linked to specific tissue histological and gene expression changes. A power analysis confirms the effectiveness of HistoGWAS in analyses of large-scale histological data, underscoring its potential to transform imaging genetic studies.

BackgroundNinety percent of the 65,000 human diseases are infrequent, collectively affecting [~] 400 million people, substantially limiting cohort accrual. This low prevalence constrains the development of robust transcriptome-based machine learning (ML) classifiers. Standard data-driven classifiers typically require cohorts of over 100 subjects per group to achieve clinical accuracy while managing high-dimensional input ([~]25,000 transcripts). These requirements are infeasible for micro-cohorts of [~]20 individuals, where overfitting becomes pervasive.

ObjectiveTo overcome these constraints, we developed a classification method that integrates three enabling strategies: (i) paired-sample transcriptome dynamics, (ii) N-of-1 pathway-based analytics, and (iii) reproducible machine learning operations (MLOps) for continuous model refinement.

MethodsUnlike ML approaches relying on a single transcriptome per subject, within-subject paired-sample designs -- such as pre-versus post-treatment or diseased versus adjacent-normal tissue -- effectively control intra-individual variability under isogenic conditions and within-subject environmental exposures (e.g. smoking history, other medications, etc.), improve signal-to-noise ratios, and, when pre-processed as single-subject studies (N-of-1), can achieve statistical power comparable to that obtained in animal models. Pathway-level N-of-1 analytics further reduces each samples high-dimensional profile into [~]4,000 biologically interpretable features, annotated with effect sizes, dispersion, and significance. Complementary MLOps practices--automated versioning, continuous monitoring, and adaptive hyperparameter tuning--improve model reproducibility and generalization.

ResultsIn two case studies--human rhinovirus infection versus matched healthy controls (n=16 training; 3 test) and breast cancer tissues harboring TP53 or PIK3CA mutations versus adjacent normal tissue (n=27 training; 9 test)--this approach achieved 90% precision and recall on an unseen breast cancer test set and 92% precision with 90% recall in rhinovirus fivefold cross-validation. Incorporating paired-sample dynamics boosted precision by 8.8% and recall by 6%, while the MLOps workflow yielded additional gains of 14.5% and 12.5%, respectively. Moreover, our method identified 42 critical gene sets (pathways) for rhinovirus response and 21 for cancer mutation status.

ConclusionsThese proof-of-concept results support the utility of integrating intra-subject dynamics, "biological knowledge"-based feature reduction (pathway-level feature reduction grounded in prior biological knowledge; e.g., N-of-1-pathways analytics), and reproducible MLOps workflows can overcome cohort-size limitations in infrequent disease, offering a scalable, interpretable solution for high-dimensional transcriptomic classification. Future work will extend these advances across various therapeutic and small-cohort designs.

In this chapter we review the relationship between genomic studies and genetics-based approaches with biomarkers for the human gut microbiota, through which the ability to carry out metagenomics and metagenome assembly paves the way for future in silico perturbations. The review includes an introduction to the use of metagenomics and metagenomics assembler software to determine the structure of the genomes, the genome content, and to map the genome to a particular location, and analyses of new types of additional data (e.g., total microbial numbers, metrics of relative abundance, annotation, etc.) which may be useful for the resolution of developmental, clinical and biological questions. It also includes a list of upstream and downstream host transcriptional programs which were confirmed by taxonomic profiling, are currently being actively interrogated with microbial transcriptomics and so can provide high-content probes for downstream consortia growth. Most importantly, it outlines the use of metagenomics and metagenomics assembler software to determine the structure of the genomes, the genome content, and to map the genome to a particular location (the primary domain of transcription or feature of the genome). This includes comprehensive description and analysis of the primary and/or secondary features of the genome and the relative abundance of each feature. Finally, this review will specifically describe the newer applications of gene expression analyses and functional data analysis, such as gene ontology and functional ontology using expression arrays and other powerful repositories, whole-genome expression quantitative methylation analysis with a phylogenetic inference approach using semi-quantitative methylomes, and bioinformatic data analysis of differential expressed genes, which have been linked to the human GI tract, as revealed in prospective studies of healthy, normal, and diseased human microbiota. Finally, we provide a list of structural tools such as the Single Molecule Analysis System and the Tachyon, as well as the numerical library on linkage such as the ASM Reference Database, GENERATOR, MetGen, and Lipin.

With growing understanding about the microbial world, including the metagenome, the microbiome, and the rhizosphere, we have learned that microbes in general are fundamental to nearly every aspect of biology, physical growth and energy production, and have been referred to as the Second Remote System after the Earth, meaning that they evolved right alongside us. Microbial dysbiosis in the human gastrointestinal (GI) tract, including the gut microbiome, is connected to a range of metabolic and inflammatory disorders. Despite its importance, the relevance of gut dysbiosis to the gut microbiome has been studied primarily in clinical trials involving fecal transplants, microbiome treatments and probiotics for chronic conditions. The amount of information gleaned from the human gut microbiome has expanded rapidly over the past decade, due to the availability of metagenomic methods to study the microbiome at genome-scale and provide an anatomical, dynamic, and spatial map of the bacterial community. The first layer of this microbiome context is dysbiosis of the gut microbiota in its geographical, temporal and temporal phylogenetic context. This axis allows for the detection of microbial group changes in direct, averaged and dynamic contexts. Linking dysbiosis to host physiology and other organ systems via the exchange of metabolites through the gut microbiome has enabled a mechanistic understanding of the relationship between microbiome and host health. Taken together, the final axis of this approach allows for understanding of the importance of host-to-microbial interactions in the microbiota context.

Community structure of gut microbiota in people with different ages of life (older and young) is presented in comparison with older-mice diet, following changes of specific bacterial members. The microbiome structure is diverse across individuals, suggesting plasticity in microbiota composition, thus may be the primary driver of age-related disease. Our aim was to identify distinct features in gut microbiota diversity that facilitate the development of newly formed gut microbiota from mouse placenta, which was pre-fed diet before birth. We evaluated community structure of microbiota in 9 individuals aged 50~70. We employed GutProMetab (https://gutproteom-dataset.com/ https://github.com/Organoids/gutproteom), a cost-efficient platform for examining complex, multi-omics datasets. The analysis of mouse gut microbiota revealed clustering of gut bacteria according to age, while individual age differences were minimal. Community structure of microbiota from 1-year old mouse placenta revealed significantly higher diversity in order to community (>5% similarity); whereas median species complexity increased in order to higher generation distance (0.43 D) from mouse placenta with developmental restriction: from 1-year old mouse to 30 years old mouse (2329 spp vs 15,548 spp). The highest of species richness was found in mice aged 30~60. The similarity of bacterial composition between individuals with multiple different durations of mouse gestation was low, but similarities were preserved over 35 years of age. Based on the highest of mammalian taxonomic units, we curated database of mouse microbiota from gestational age 1-30 years, which makes it possible to perform future longitudinal studies using microbiota profiling for age-related studies. The results suggested that the difference of genera composition between mouse placenta and mouse population may be associated with diet changes and environmental factors.

The microbiome has a central role in human physiology and health, primarily because human microbiota contribute to the development of immune responses, and the diversity and composition of microbiota within individuals predispose them to specific health conditions. As a result, the gut microbiota and the microbiome interact intimately with the human gut. Gut microbiota are predictive of intestinal inflammation and composition in type 2 diabetes, but mechanisms of how gut microbiota interact with the human microbiome remain largely unclear. Here we focus on the fecal 16S rRNA, measuring the composition of the gut microbiome from stool samples from 16 participants. We observed that the number of bacterial species isolated from the stool is correlated with an increase in the fecal 16S rRNA to reflect the selective pressure of gut microbiota on our microbiome. We performed microbial-level analysis on the identified species from the gut microbiota and analysed its transcriptional network. We propose that many species change the transcriptomes of relevant pathways linked to the aforementioned human conditions and use the 16S rRNA data for further analyses. A total of 169 species were identified, of which 142 had a statistically significant enrichment, but no evidence of causality. None of the identified species were enriched for bacteria from stomach flora.

A common adverse event is B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), which can be rapidly fatal if untreated. Previous studies from several laboratory settings established that exposure to the gut microbiota can synergize with small-molecule drugs and oncogenic viruses in inducing B-ALL. This study aimed to identify a strain of commensal Prevotellaprotirumandhow its commensal capacity impacted the induction of B-ALL. We targeted glycolipids and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) involved in modulating immune homeostasis using genome editing and live cell microscopy, followed by co-culturing with patient and control colon cancer cell lines. We then quantified the colonization of Prevotella in the colon compared to patients using the in-house strain-specific screening method for commensal bacteria. P.protidata is a common commensal bacteria of the Prevotella genus. We observed that the strain P.protidata was inversely associated with disease phenotypes, while the intestinal commensal bacteria P.olimicola and P.prorosevere. Among them, P.protidatapossesses the highest ability to colonize and culture at the p.protidata-enrichment strain of the colon. Our in vivo live-cell microscopy observations and correlation between the results demonstrated that the metabolic role of metabolites derived from tryptophan, alongside the glycosaminoglycans in the mucus and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) metabolism, were pivotal in exacerbating Burkitt cell/leukaemia and natural killer-mediated immune therapy.

BackgroundProbiotics are live microbial feed additives and immunomodulating compounds. Several exogenous microbes are known to modulate gut microflora, thus influencing the homeostasis of the gastrointestinal tract. Although certain probiotic strains are routinely used in ruminant dairy production, it remains unclear if probiotic effects are mainly confined to a microbial population. Using metagenomics- and chemical characterization-based methods, we aimed to further define the microbiome composition in the experimental cohort and investigate the effect of probiotics on mouse cecal microbiota. Moreover, the relationship between probiotic supplements and weight loss was also tested by conducting a meta-analysis.

MethodsMaintained mice were administered probiotic supplements (PROBIOTIC-G) for four weeks. The median and IQR values of cecal microbiota composition were assessed weekly, and the cecal microbiota was analyzed using high-throughput pyrosequencing and metabolomics to understand probiotic effects. Further, the effect of probiotics on mice was tested using a short-term experimental breeding program for rumen-induced weight loss (RUW). For microbiota analysis, volatile gases, fecal gas samples, and fecal pellets were collected from mice at post-methane and post-fermentation periods.

ResultsWithin the mouse microbiome, Nannoploid bifidobacterium species was most abundant, whereas Rhizobiales and Oxalobacteriaceae, two known probiotic species, were rare. Probiotic supplements significantly influenced the composition of the mouse microbiome at the genus level (FDR=0.0022, least-significant difference: P=0.02). Within each genus, probiotic supplementation substantially influenced specific microbes, particularly Nannoploid bifidbacteria. The effect of probiotics on weight loss (5750~\u2009kg) was investigated using a factorial experimental breeding program based on a two-factor summary (probiotic and blank). Compared to that of the blank, probiotics caused 75% to 93% changes (mean \u2009kg) on obese mice.

ConclusionThe findings of our study offer compelling evidence for the therapeutic efficacy of probiotic supplements in preventing the obesity-related effects in mice. Additionally, they highlight the potential of probiotics as a dietary intervention for body weight management.

Gut bacteria serve as the foundational microbiota in the human gut and in most other mammals. They possess an ancient biosynthetic core such as short chain fatty acids, but can also secrete sophisticated secondary metabolites capable of disrupting signaling pathways that control host metabolism. We used a metabolic screen to identify candidate probiotic bacteria that secrete new metabolite pathways and induced the production of secondary metabolite types in a human gut model. We discovered that a novel short chain fatty acid and branched chain fatty acid synthase from a strain of the Bacteroidetes pathogenic bacterium Prevotella savini showed physiological effects in gut models. We identified the key metabolisms by which these two new microorganisms enhanced the expression of secondary metabolite pathways and provided an absolute screen of candidate probiotics and probiotic-derived products for specific secondary metabolite pathways. Probiotic bacteria secrete many novel species of secondary metabolites with physiological effects on host metabolism in our gut model.

The inflammatory response to intestinal pathogens and their infection site remains poorly understood. This is due to the complex dynamics of mucosal epithelial composition and immune cell composition in the colon. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses of commensal commensal bacteria of the human colon have previously shed light on the immunological response to enteric bacteria, but limited diversity among the microbial community, in particular between the microbiota of the GALT and the intestine, has been reported. To identify the molecular factors regulating the microbiota in the intestine, we performed single-cell RNAseq in the human intestine together with a murine model of colitis. A metabolite profile from the intra-intestinal microbiome derived from the GALT and a microbiome study of the human intestine were combined with single cell transcriptomic analyses to identify important metabolic pathways. We found that the microbiota of the murine colitis model contains commensals and that their metabolic pathways are similar to that of the human GALT. Using bioinformatics analyses, we identified metabolic parameters in the murine commensals that were highly correlated with the metabolites of the human GALT. We used this information to identify target genes in the GALT microbiota and identified a metabolic pathway regulated by the commensal Faecalibacterium-derived butyrate during faecal handling. This study underlines the synergistic contribution of the microbiota and the intestinal environment to the functional induction of faecalibacterium-derived metabolites.

The human gut harbors a rich and complex ecology of commensal microbes. Thus, the interaction between microbiota and host may either exert beneficial effects or generate harmful side effects, such as obesity and diabetes. These side effects are due in part to the gastrointestinal microbiota's ability to produce metabolites, which influence host health and functionality. While metabolites produced by the microbiota have received much recent attention, it is not known whether the relationship between microbiome-derived metabolites and intestinal health are both indirect and more complex than the classic inverse association. We address this question in two independent reports. First, we utilize our human commensal cohorts to measure intestinal microbiome metabolism and investigate its relationship with measured body weight and biomarkers of metabolic disease. We observed that the host's weight was not a linear proxy for body weight but rather a sub-linear relationship with carbon monooxygenation and carbon dioxide production. Additionally, we discovered that the accumulation of carbon monooxygenation markers within a healthy individual closely predicted body weight, regardless of the host's weight-bearing or overall health. Conversely, accumulation of carbon dioxide production markers, which are known to be linked to metabolic disease, did not correlate with body weight. Next, we utilized the human cohort to explore other potential pathways by which the microbiota may manipulate gut microbiome metabolite profiles. We evaluated the microbiota metabolite composition and generation time to measure the distance between microbiota-derived metabolites and possible host-derived biosynthetic pathways. Importantly, we found that alterations in metabolite generation time had a marked tendency to correlate with metabolism, suggesting that the gut microbiome may be priming metabolic health through metabolite generation. Overall, our results indicated that a commensal microbiota-derived product exerts a portion of the pathophysiological benefits of its metabolic product. Our results thus confirm that the microbiota mediates many of the gut-host interactions that ultimately influence metabolite production.

Sugar abundance during early childhood has been shown to be an important determinant of the general development and plasticity of the microbiome. The commensal gut microbiome influences brain function through the gastrointestinal tract (GIA), including aspects of immunity and learning. However, distinct gut and brain populations of the microbiome are poorly understood due to sampling bias and tissue complexity of microbiota-brain interactions. This study aimed to elucidate the gut-brain-metabolism nexus through a comparative study of obese, non-obese, and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) child and adult mice. Using a metabolomics-based research approach, we confirmed species- and tissue-based alterations in metabolic dysregulation and panel dysbiosis between obese and non-obese mice. For the IBD mice, we observed a specific immune panel reaction to colitis, including inflammation, eosinophilic uptake, and the production of short chain fatty acids. We utilized the genus that has a specific immune response to colitis, Arcanobacterium, as a reference strain in this case, and with Coagulase-Negative Staphylococci (CNS) as the reference strain, we identified Arcanobacterium novocasta to be the putative dysbiosis inducing the distinct immune response, revealing a general host immune dysregulation related to the gut microbiome. Additionally, we evaluated the dysbiosis of the two strains using shotgun proteomics and the metabolites identified as Coagulase Negative Staphylococci-like proteins, which are thought to be anti-inflammatory peptides for the benefit of immune-mediated colitis.
